alt: Rapid growth puts pressure on food, water, housing, schools, jobs and the environment, so some governments aim to slow it. Low fertility and ageing leave fewer workers to support the elderly, so others want more births or more immigrants. Every strategy changes births or migration, never deaths.
caption: Governments manage population for opposite reasons, but always through births or migration.

alt: Five strategies feed into two levers. Access to contraception, population policies, access to education and access to healthcare act on births. Control of migration, through visas, permits, quotas and points systems, acts on migration. Deaths are not a lever.
caption: Four strategies act on births and one on migration; none acts through deaths.

alt: Side-by-side comparison. Pro-natalist policies, such as France’s family benefits, use payments, tax cuts, parental leave, childcare and housing priority; they can slow decline but are expensive, often have small effects and take about 20 years to add workers. Anti-natalist policies, such as China’s one-child policy from around 1980 to 2015, use campaigns, incentives, penalties or legal limits; they can lower births quickly but raise ethical concerns and, in China, skewed the sex ratio and sped up ageing.
caption: Pro-natalist means more births, anti-natalist fewer; each has costs and side effects.

alt: A timeline for Singapore. In the 1970s a Stop at Two campaign aimed to lower births. Fertility then fell very low, so in the late 1980s the government switched to measures encouraging larger families.
caption: Singapore moved from anti-natalist to pro-natalist within about a generation.

alt: Two chains. Education: girls stay in school longer, so they marry and start families later, have better jobs, know more about contraception and have more say, so fertility falls, but slowly. Healthcare: fewer children die, so parents need fewer extra children and clinics deliver contraception, so fertility falls, though in the short term growth can rise because deaths fall first.
caption: Education and healthcare lower fertility indirectly; both take time, and healthcare first raises growth.

alt: A scale from fast to slow. Control of migration works quickly and anti-natalist policies can lower births quickly; pro-natalist births take about 20 years to join the workforce; education works when pupils become adults. Other questions to ask: voluntary or compulsory, cost, side effects and fit with the country.
caption: Speed is one test of a strategy; also weigh cost, compulsion, side effects and fit.

after: ## Worked example 1: measuring a policy's effect
alt: Bars show fertility falling from 5.2 to 3.1 children per woman over 15 years after a contraception and girls’ education programme, a fall of 2.1 or 40.4%. A dashed line at about 2.1 marks replacement level; 3.1 is still above it, so the population keeps growing more slowly.
caption: A 40.4% fall in fertility still leaves it above replacement, so growth slows but continues.
